title: Most people think the Pharisees were condemned because they were openly sinful.
paragraphs: Most people think the Pharisees were condemned because they were openly sinful.
But that is not the truth.
The Pharisees were condemned because they looked holy while loving applause more than God.

They prayed.
They taught Scripture.
They fasted.
They followed religious rules with extreme discipline.
From the outside, they looked like the most devoted people in society.
But Jesus saw something deeper.
He saw the hidden hunger inside their hearts.
They didn’t just want to serve God.
They wanted people to notice them serving God.

They loved the important seats in public gatherings.
They loved the respectful greetings in marketplaces.
They loved the titles that made people admire them.
And slowly, without realizing it, their desire for recognition replaced their desire for righteousness.
That is the lesson the Pharisees teach us.
And it is far more relevant today than most people realize.
Because human nature has not changed.
Even in spiritual spaces, the heart can begin craving something dangerous:
Recognition.

We want to be seen as wise.
We want to be seen as faithful.
We want to be seen as spiritual.
But when the desire to appear righteous becomes stronger than the desire to be righteous, the soul begins to drift.
This is why Jesus spoke some of His strongest warnings to the Pharisees.
Not because they rejected religion.
But because they turned religion into a performance.
They polished the outside of the cup.
But inside, pride was growing quietly.
And that warning still echoes today.
Because a person can know Scripture and still crave admiration.
A person can serve in ministry and still secretly hope people notice them.
A person can speak about humility while silently enjoying the praise that follows.
And here is the uncomfortable truth:
Public praise can slowly replace private purity.
At first it feels harmless.
Someone compliments your faith.
Someone applauds your leadership.
Someone admires your wisdom.
But if the heart is not guarded, something subtle happens.
You begin feeding on that applause.
And when that happens, the motivation slowly shifts.
You are no longer serving God alone.
You are serving the image of being admired.
The Pharisees remind us that spiritual pride often wears religious clothing.
It speaks the right language.
It stands in the right places.
It performs the right actions.
But beneath the surface, the heart is craving something other than God.
And Jesus exposed that reality.
He said they loved human praise more than the praise that comes from God.
Think about that for a moment.
They preferred the approval of people over the approval of heaven.
And that is a terrifying exchange.
Because human applause is loud, but it fades quickly.
God’s approval is quiet, but it lasts forever.
The Pharisees built reputations that impressed crowds.
But Jesus looked straight through the reputation and saw the heart.
And that is the part of this story that should humble all of us.
Because the temptation to perform spiritually still exists.
Especially in a world where everything can be seen.
Where platforms are public.
Where faith can be displayed.
Where recognition can come instantly.
It is possible to build a public image of devotion while neglecting the private place where God actually shapes a person.
But God is not looking for impressive appearances.
He is looking for surrendered hearts.
He is not impressed by titles.
He is not moved by public recognition.
He looks at what happens when no one is watching.
When the crowd is gone.
When the spotlight disappears.
When the only audience left is heaven.
That is where real faith lives.
The Pharisees teach us a lesson that every believer must wrestle with:
It is possible to look close to God while being far from Him.
That is why humility matters.
That is why secret prayer matters.
That is why obedience in hidden places matters.
Because the truest faith is not the one that attracts applause.
The truest faith is the one that would still obey God even if nobody noticed.
Even if nobody praised it.
Even if nobody celebrated it.
Because at the end of the day, one question matters more than every title, compliment, or reputation.
Not:
“Did people admire me?”
But:
“Was God pleased with my heart?”
The Pharisees chased admiration.
But Jesus calls us to something deeper.
Not performance.
Not reputation.
Not applause.
But quiet, genuine surrender.
And the people God trusts the most are often not the ones standing in the brightest spotlight.
They are the ones faithfully walking with Him in the shadows where only God can see.
Because the greatest reward is not public praise.
The greatest reward is hearing God say:
“Well done.”
Scripture

Matthew 23:5–7
“Everything they do is done for people to see…”

Have you ever caught yourself wanting recognition for doing something spiritual?
